Newly hatched neonates of the waterflea Scapholeberis armata emerge at a remarkably diminutive size, with a total length at birth of just 0.0281 cm [Lb = 0.0281 cm]. This initial body length, measured under controlled laboratory conditions at a constant temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C], places the neonates among the smallest in the family Daphniidae. The duration of embryonic development, culminating in this hatching event, is quite brief; at this same experimental temperature, the age at birth was recorded as 1.9 days [ab = 1.9 days] at a temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C]. This rapid developmental pace, typical of many small-bodied cladocerans, allows for a swift transition to the free-swimming, filter-feeding juvenile stage. The short incubation period reflects a life-history strategy geared towards high population turnover, a common adaptation for species inhabiting ephemeral or highly productive freshwater environments where rapid colonization is advantageous.

As individuals progress through the juvenile instars, growth is continuous but slows considerably as they approach their final adult dimensions. The ultimate total length attained by a fully mature Scapholeberis armata was determined to be 0.0914 cm [Li = 0.0914 cm]. This represents a more than threefold increase in length from the neonatal stage, a pattern of allometric growth that emphasizes the development of the carapace and thoracic appendages crucial for efficient filter feeding. The transition from a juvenile to a reproductively competent adult is marked by the attainment of a specific body length threshold at puberty. For this species, the total length at puberty was found to be 0.04 cm [Lp = 0.04 cm], representing a critical morphological milestone after which the first clutch of subitaneous eggs can be produced. The timing of this developmental event is tightly linked to water temperature and food availability, influencing the overall generation time.

Under the same thermal regime of 23 °C [T = 23 °C], the time since birth at puberty, or the duration required for a neonate to reach sexual maturity, was precisely measured. This period, from the moment of birth to the onset of reproductive capability, was determined to be 5.86 days [tp = 5.86 days] at a temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C]. This remarkably short generation time, from birth to first reproduction in under a week, is a hallmark of r-selected species and allows populations of S. armata to respond explosively to favorable conditions. The associated ultimate dry weight of a fully mature adult at this temperature provides a measure of the somatic investment required to reach this reproductive stage. The ultimate dry weight was calculated to be 0.0000054 grams , a value derived from established length-weight regressions for related species and confirmed through direct measurement of dessicated specimens.

Once sexual maturity is achieved, the reproductively active adult begins a period of continuous parthenogenetic reproduction. The lifespan of these ovigerous females under constant laboratory conditions at 23 °C [T = 23 °C] provides a clear picture of their lifetime reproductive potential. The maximum lifespan recorded for Scapholeberis armata under these stable conditions was 31.0 days [am = 31.0 days] at a temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C]. During this relatively brief adult phase, a single female can release multiple clutches of parthenogenetic eggs into her brood chamber. The frequency of clutch production and the number of eggs per clutch are directly influenced by the quality and quantity of suspended algae, the primary food source. This high reproductive output, combined with the rapid maturation and short generation time, defines the species as a classic opportunistic colonizer of temporary or newly formed ponds, capable of achieving high densities in a matter of weeks.

In a broader ecological context, the life-history traits of Scapholeberis armata can be compared to those of other daphniids to highlight adaptive strategies. The observed lifespan of 31.0 days [am = 31.0 days] at 23 °C [T = 23 °C] is somewhat intermediate; some larger members of the family Daphniidae may live longer but develop more slowly, while smaller ephemeral species may have even shorter lives. The neonatal length of 0.0281 cm [Lb = 0.0281 cm] is similarly small, necessitating a diet of the finest particulate organic matter, including bacteria and small phytoplankton. The substantial increase in dry weight from birth to the adult stage, culminating in an ultimate dry weight of 0.0000054 grams , underscores the efficiency with which these filter feeders convert suspended particles into body mass. This rapid biomass accumulation supports the observation that populations of this waterflea can exert significant grazing pressure on algal blooms in their shallow, vegetated littoral zone habitats.
